Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses exposition and summary in the opening sections to establish the characters, their domestic life, the history and atmosphere of Congregation Ohr Tamid, and the beloved nature of Rabbi Adler. This background information creates emotional stakes without bogging down the narrative. When the central conflict arrives—the shooting and the subsequent panic in the sanctuary and lobby—the story seamlessly transitions into vivid, real-time scenes filled with sensory details, physical action, and brief, tense dialogue. Finally, the story uses summary to bridge the time gap between the immediate aftermath in the lobby and the drive to the hospital later that afternoon, allowing the story to conclude with one final, quiet scene in the car.
